pos: adv. (to a very great degree; beyond what is usual or expected)
etymology: From exceed, Latin excedere, to go out beyond, with the adverbial ending. In the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew intensive me'od me'od (very, very) and the Greek compounds built on huper, beyond.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version's strongest ordinary intensifier, and the striking thing about it is how evenly it is distributed between God's blessing and man's sin. It carries the flood: “And the waters prevailed exceedingly upon the earth” (Gen 7:19). It carries the covenant: God tells Abram, “I will make my covenant between me and thee, and will multiply thee exceedingly” (Gen 17:2). It carries Sodom: “But the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the LORD exceedingly” (Gen 13:13). It carries Jonah's mariners, who were exceedingly afraid; Paul before conversion, who was exceedingly mad against the saints; and Moses at Sinai, who confessed, “I exceedingly fear and quake.” A word this strong is not scattered lightly, and its placement is instructive. Scripture does not use it to describe a comfortable religious feeling. It uses it where something has passed the ordinary bounds — a judgment that overtops the hills, a promise that overtops arithmetic, a wickedness that overtops what the land will bear, a fear that overtops a prophet's composure. The word marks the point at which a creature runs out of measure, and it is used of God's dealings far more than of man's feelings.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exceedingly as to a very great degree; in a degree beyond what is usual; greatly; very much.
webster_full: EXCEEDINGLY, adv. To a very great degree; in a degree beyond what is usual; greatly; very much.
2. In a degree exceeding or surpassing something else, or the common measure.
3. Applied both to what is good and to what is evil, the word marks only the degree, not the quality.
corruption_summary: A generation that calls everything amazing has no word left for what is actually beyond measure, and the flattening runs in one direction only — upward on trifles and downward on sin.
corruption_paragraphs: Language inflates the way currency does, and for the same reason: the more freely a strong word is spent, the less it will buy. Ordinary modern speech now applies the superlatives to lunch, to weather, to a passing convenience, so that when a man comes to speak of the holiness of God or the weight of his own guilt he finds the vocabulary already spent. The Authorized Version guards against this by rationing. It says exceedingly of the flood, of the covenant with Abram, of the wickedness of Sodom, and of Moses trembling at the mount — and having spent it there, it does not spend it on small things. The corruption is not merely stylistic. Genesis 13:13 sets the two men of the passage side by side: Sodom is wicked exceedingly, and Abram is promised increase exceedingly, and the reader is meant to feel that both statements are of the same order of seriousness. A culture that will still say exceedingly of a pleasure but never of a sin has not become kinder; it has simply lost half the scale, and with it the ability to hear either the warning or the promise at full weight.
roots_summary: Hebrew me'od (H3966), muchness, force, doubled for the superlative; Greek sphodra (G4970), vehemently; and the huper- compounds Paul coins for what runs past measure.
roots_lines: Hebrew me'od (H3966) — might, muchness; doubled as me'od me'od it is the Hebrew superlative, and it is the word behind the flood prevailing exceedingly; Genesis 7:19.
Greek sphodra (G4970) — vehemently, very much; used of the disciples' sorrow and of the exceeding great joy of the wise men; Matthew 2:10.
Greek huperperissos and its kin (G5249) — beyond all measure; Paul's habit of stacking huper on an already strong word when the subject is grace; Ephesians 3:20.
usage: “The waters prevailed exceedingly upon the earth” — the word measuring a judgment that overtops the hills.
“The men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the LORD exceedingly” — the same weight laid on sin.
“I exceedingly fear and quake” — Moses at the mount, quoted by the writer to the Hebrews.
scriptures: Gen 7:19
And the waters prevailed exceedingly upon the earth; and all the high hills, that were under the whole heaven, were covered.
But the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the LORD exceedingly.
And so terrible was the sight, that Moses said, I exceedingly fear and quake:)

pos: adv. (speedily; without delay; suddenly)
etymology: Old English cwic, living, alive — the sense of speed is secondary to the sense of life, as in the quick and the dead. The Greek tachu carries suddenness rather than mere haste.
biblical_def: Two things in Scripture are said to happen quickly, and they answer to one another. The first is apostasy. Moses comes down the mount and finds the calf: “ye had turned aside quickly out of the way which the LORD had commanded you” (Deu 9:16). Joshua warns that a covenant-breaking nation shall perish quickly from off the good land. The speed with which a people can leave the God who has just delivered them is one of the plainest facts of the Old Testament, and it is stated as a warning, not as a curiosity. The second is the Lord's coming. To Ephesus: “I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent” (Rev 2:5). And at the very end, in the last words the ascended Christ speaks in the canon: “Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus” (Rev 22:20). The Greek tachu in these places does not promise a short interval on a calendar; it promises a coming that will be sudden when it comes, and it is set against the slowness of a church that means to repent later.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines quickly as speedily; with haste or celerity; soon; without delay.
webster_full: QUICKLY, adv. Speedily; with haste or celerity.
2. Soon; without delay.
3. In a short time; shortly after the present or a given time.
corruption_summary: The mocker's question — where is the promise of his coming? — treats quickly as a failed prediction of date, when Scripture uses it of suddenness and of the shortness of the sinner's reprieve.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter answered this objection before it was raised. Scoffers would come saying that all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation, and the apostle's reply is not that the interval is short but that the interval is mercy: the Lord is not slack concerning his promise, but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish. The quickly of Revelation belongs to the same logic as the thief in the night — a word about manner, not about the length of the wait. Two readings corrupt it in opposite directions. Full preterism resolves the difficulty by declaring every promise already fulfilled in the first century, which empties the church's hope of a bodily return. Date-setting resolves it by making quickly a measurable countdown, and has been falsified in every generation that has tried it, from the Millerites forward. The Authorized Version's own instinct is better: the word is set at the end of the book as a comfort to a persecuted church and a summons to an unrepentant one, and the church's answer to it is not a calculation but a prayer, Even so, come, Lord Jesus.
roots_summary: Greek tachu and tacheos (G5035, G5030), swiftly, suddenly; Hebrew maher (H4116), to hasten, used of Israel's quick turning aside.
roots_lines: Hebrew maher (H4116) — to hasten, be swift; in Deuteronomy 9 it is the speed of Israel's defection, and in Exodus 32:8 the LORD Himself uses the word of them; Deuteronomy 9:16.
Greek tachu (G5035) — quickly, suddenly; the word in the letters to the seven churches and in the last promise of the canon; Revelation 22:20.
Greek en tachei (G5034) — in speed, shortly; the opening words of the Revelation, things which must shortly come to pass; Revelation 1:1.
usage: “Ye had turned aside quickly out of the way” — the speed of apostasy, stated as a warning.
“I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick” — the threat to a church, not to the world.
“Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus” — the last exchange in Scripture.
scriptures: Deu 9:16
And I looked, and, behold, ye had sinned against the LORD your God, and had made you a molten calf: ye had turned aside quickly out of the way which the LORD had commanded you.
Rev 2:5
Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.
He which testifieth these things saith, Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus.

pos: adv. (in a great degree or plentiful measure; more than sufficiently)
etymology: Latin abundare, to overflow — literally to rise in waves, from unda, a wave. The image is of water going over the brim, which is exactly how Genesis first uses it.
biblical_def: The first use sets the picture: “And God said, Let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creature that hath life” (Gen 1:20). The word belongs to a Creator whose ordinary way of working is overflow — not the bare minimum that would suffice, but swarming, teeming life. The plagues run the same word backwards: the river shall bring forth frogs abundantly, and the reader is meant to feel that the fertility which was a blessing has become a judgment. In the Psalms it moves to speech: “They shall abundantly utter the memory of thy great goodness” (Psa 145:7). In the New Testament it settles on two things. First, the life Christ gives: “I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly” (Joh 10:10) — said in the same breath as the thief who comes to steal and kill, so that the abundance is defined against the shepherd's laying down of His life, three verses later. Second, the entrance into the kingdom: an entrance shall be ministered unto you abundantly, which Peter attaches to diligence in adding grace to grace.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines abundantly as fully; amply; plentifully; in a sufficient degree, and more.
webster_full: ABUNDANTLY, adv. Fully; amply; plentifully; in a sufficient degree.
2. Copiously; in great numbers or quantity.
3. Used of that which is more than enough, as the waters brought forth abundantly.
corruption_summary: John 10:10 has been detached from its own paragraph and made a promise of material increase, when the abundance Christ names is defined three verses later by the shepherd giving His life for the sheep.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is quoted as a slogan more often than it is read as a sentence. In context the Lord is contrasting Himself with thieves and hirelings who come for the flock's wool and not the flock's good, and the abundance He offers is expounded immediately: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep. The abundant life is therefore first of all a life secured by a death — eternal life, resurrection life, the life of a sheep that shall never perish and out of whose hand none shall pluck. The prosperity teaching of the last century, from Kenyon and Hagin through the present television ministries, reverses this: the abundance becomes health, income, and the removal of hardship, and the death of the shepherd drops out of the paragraph entirely. The test is simple and historical. The men who first heard the promise were the apostles, and the New Testament records what abundance they received — imprisonments, stripes, shipwreck, and martyrdom — while insisting in the same documents that they had all things and abounded. Paul, who had learned in whatsoever state he was therewith to be content, is the apostolic commentary on the word.
roots_summary: Hebrew sharats (H8317), to swarm, teem; Greek perissos (G4053), over and above, exceeding what is necessary; plousios (G4146), richly.
roots_lines: Hebrew sharats (H8317) — to swarm, to bring forth in teeming numbers; the fifth day of creation and the frogs of the second plague use the same verb; Genesis 1:20, Exodus 8:3.
Greek perissos (G4053) — over and above, more than enough; the comparative in John 10:10 is perisson, abundance beyond the bare having of life; John 10:10.
Greek plousios (G4146) — richly; the entrance ministered abundantly into the everlasting kingdom, and the word of Christ dwelling in you richly; 2 Peter 1:11, Colossians 3:16.
usage: “Let the waters bring forth abundantly” — the Creator's ordinary way of working is overflow.
“That they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly” — read with verse 11.
“An entrance shall be ministered unto you abundantly” — Peter, on diligence adding grace to grace.
scriptures: Gen 1:20
And God said, Let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creature that hath life, and fowl that may fly above the earth in the open firmament of heaven.
The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.
For so an entrance shall be ministered unto you abundantly into the everlasting kingdom of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.

pos: adv. (without doubt or question; assuredly; in truth)
etymology: Latin certus, settled, decided, from cernere, to sift or decide. In the Old Testament it most often renders the Hebrew infinitive absolute, a doubling of the verb which the translators render surely or certainly.
biblical_def: The word carries God's own oath-language into English. At the bush, when Moses asks who am I, the answer does not tell him who he is: “And he said, Certainly I will be with thee; and this shall be a token unto thee, that I have sent thee” (Exo 3:12). The certainty is transferred from the man to the God who sends him, which is the pattern of every biblical commission. The same construction underlies the promise to Abraham that God will certainly return, and the warning through Jeremiah to the remnant determined on Egypt: “Now therefore know certainly that ye shall die by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence” (Jer 42:22). The word is used for judgment as freely as for promise, because both rest on the same divine veracity. At the cross a Roman officer, who had no covenant and no scriptures, reaches the word by another road: “Certainly this was a righteous man” (Luk 23:47). Luke puts it as a verdict, and the reader is meant to notice that the centurion is certain of what the Sanhedrin had voted itself uncertain about.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines certainly as without doubt or question; in truth and fact; without failure.
webster_full: CERTAINLY, adv. Without doubt or question; in truth and fact.
2. Without failure; as, he will certainly come.
3. Used to affirm a thing with confidence, on evidence which admits no doubt.
corruption_summary: The age treats certainty itself as a species of arrogance, so that a man may hold any conviction he pleases provided he holds it loosely — which is the one condition Scripture never grants.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a real vice near this virtue, and Scripture names it: the man who is wise in his own conceit, the false prophet who says thus saith the LORD when the LORD has not spoken, the Corinthian who knows and is puffed up. Humility about our own understanding is a genuine duty. But the modern move is different in kind. It relocates the vice from the ground of a claim to the firmness of it, so that confidence as such becomes the fault and tentativeness as such becomes the virtue. Scripture will not have this. The whole of Luke's Gospel is written that Theophilus might know the certainty of those things wherein he had been instructed; Paul knows whom he has believed and is persuaded; John writes that ye may know that ye have eternal life. The apostolic register is not one of held opinions but of settled knowledge. The proper correction to false certainty is not less certainty but better ground — God who cannot lie, and a testimony given in history and confirmed by witnesses. A faith that has been talked out of its assurance in the name of humility has not become more modest about itself; it has become more modest about God.
roots_summary: Hebrew infinitive absolute doubling (as yadoa teda, knowing thou shalt know); Greek ontos (G3689), really, in truth; asphaleia (G803), safety, certainty.
roots_lines: Hebrew infinitive absolute — the verb doubled for emphasis, rendered surely or certainly by the translators; the construction behind God's oath to Abraham and His sentence on the remnant in Egypt; Jeremiah 42:22.
Greek ontos (G3689) — really, actually, in very deed; the centurion's word at the cross in Luke's account; Luke 23:47.
Greek asphaleia (G803) — that which cannot be made to slip; Luke's stated purpose in writing, that thou mightest know the certainty; Luke 1:4.
usage: “Certainly I will be with thee” — the answer to who am I is about God, not about Moses.
“Know certainly that ye shall die by the sword” — the same veracity behind the warning as behind the promise.
“Certainly this was a righteous man” — the centurion's verdict against the council's.
scriptures: Exo 3:12
And he said, Certainly I will be with thee; and this shall be a token unto thee, that I have sent thee: When thou hast brought forth the people out of Egypt, ye shall serve God upon this mountain.
Now therefore know certainly that ye shall die by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence, in the place whither ye desire to go and to sojourn.
Now when the centurion saw what was done, he glorified God, saying, Certainly this was a righteous man.

pos: adv. (completely; entirely; without lack or reservation)
etymology: Old English full with the adverbial ending. In the Greek it stands for compounds in pleero- (to fill up) and plero-phoreo, to be carried to full measure — the word for a ship under full sail.
biblical_def: A small word doing decisive work. Luke marks the arrival of Pentecost with it: “And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place” (Act 2:1) — the fulness is of time, the appointed day having run out its measure. Moses is said to have fully set up the tabernacle before the anointing; nothing partial could be consecrated. Paul asks for the same completeness in the conscience: “Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind” (Rom 14:5), which in a chapter about days and meats is not a licence for indifference but a demand that a man's practice rest on settled conviction rather than on the pressure of his neighbours. And Solomon turns the word toward evil: “Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil” (Ecc 8:11). That is the whole doctrine of hardened sin in one line. Delay in judgment is read by the sinner as absence of judgment, and the heart, finding no immediate resistance, settles into its course completely.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fully as completely; entirely; without deficiency; to the full extent.
webster_full: FULLY, adv. Completely; entirely; without deficiency.
2. To the full extent or measure; as, fully persuaded.
3. Abundantly; plentifully.
corruption_summary: Ecclesiastes 8:11 names the mechanism by which a delayed judgment is mistaken for no judgment at all, and the heart, meeting no immediate check, sets itself completely in the way it has chosen.
corruption_paragraphs: Solomon is not describing a peculiar wickedness but an ordinary one, and the observation is psychological before it is theological. A sentence not executed speedily teaches the sinner, by the plainest experiment he knows, that the thing may be done with impunity; and having taught him that once, it teaches him it more firmly each time. The heart is then fully set — not tempted, not inclined, but settled. The same forbearance that Romans 2 calls the goodness of God leading to repentance is here turned by the sinner into evidence that repentance is unnecessary, which is why Paul asks in that chapter whether a man despises the riches of God's longsuffering. The pastoral application cuts against a common assumption. Men suppose that a striking providence — an illness, a loss, an exposure — is what hardens the heart, and that God's kindness softens it. Ecclesiastes says the reverse is at least as common: it is precisely the uninterrupted run of prosperous sinning that fixes a man. That is why the delay in judgment is nowhere in Scripture offered as a comfort to the impenitent, and why Peter, having granted that a thousand years are as a day, immediately says the day of the Lord will come as a thief.
roots_summary: Greek pleroo (G4137), to fill, to complete; plerophoreo (G4135), to carry to full measure, hence to be fully persuaded; Hebrew male (H4390), to be full.
roots_lines: Hebrew male (H4390) — to be full, to fill up; used of a completed period of days and of the tabernacle fully set up; Numbers 7:1.
Greek sumpleroo (G4845) — to fill up completely; Luke's verb for the day of Pentecost being fully come, the appointed time having run out; Acts 2:1.
Greek plerophoreo (G4135) — to bear to fulness, to persuade completely; behind Romans 14:5 and Abraham being fully persuaded that what God had promised He was able to perform; Romans 4:21.
usage: “When the day of Pentecost was fully come” — an appointed time having run out its measure.
“Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind” — conviction, not indifference.
“The heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil” — delay read as acquittal.
scriptures: Act 2:1
And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place.
Rom 14:5
One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.
Ecc 8:11
Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil.

pos: adv. (with kindness; benevolently; also adj., natural, according to kind)
etymology: Old English gecyndelic, natural, according to one's kind — the older sense survives in kindly fruits of the earth. The moral sense follows: to act kindly is to act as one of the same kind.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version has a habit with this word that is easy to miss and hard to unlearn once seen: it almost never lets kindly stand alone. Abraham's servant asks Laban and Bethuel, “if ye will deal kindly and truly with my master, tell me” (Gen 24:49). Jacob asks the same of Joseph, deal kindly and truly with me. The spies swear it to Rahab, we will deal kindly and truly with thee. The pairing is not decoration; it is the Hebrew chesed we-emeth, covenant-love and faithfulness, the two together, and the second word is what keeps the first from being sentiment. Naomi blesses her daughters in law with it: “The LORD deal kindly with you, as ye have dealt with the dead, and with me” (Rut 1:8). In the New Testament Paul makes it a family word: “Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another” (Rom 12:10) — where the Greek compounds the word for family affection, so that the church is to feel toward one another what kinsmen feel, and then to go past it in giving honour away.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines kindly as with good will; with a disposition to make others happy or to oblige; benevolently; and in the older sense, according to nature or kind.
webster_full: KINDLY, adv. With good will; with a disposition to make others happy, or to oblige; benevolently; favorably.
KINDLY, a. Homogeneal; congenial; of the same nature.
2. Mild; bland; softening; as kindly showers.
corruption_summary: Kindness severed from truth becomes mere agreeableness, and the Authorized Version's persistent pairing — kindly and truly — is the standing correction to it.
corruption_paragraphs: Four times in the narrative books the phrase runs the same way: deal kindly and truly. The Hebrew behind it, chesed we-emeth, is the pair that Exodus 34 puts in God's own self-description — abundant in goodness and truth — and that John 1:14 carries into Greek when the Word is full of grace and truth. The two are given together because either one alone deforms. Truth without kindness is the accuracy of an enemy. Kindness without truth is what a man offers when he has decided that the other party cannot bear reality, and it is therefore a quiet form of contempt. The therapeutic register of the present hour makes the second error systematically: to be kind is redefined as to affirm, and to withhold agreement is redefined as a species of harm, with the result that the only remaining way to love a man is to tell him nothing he does not already believe. Scripture's categories are firmer and gentler at once. Faithful are the wounds of a friend, says Proverbs, and the deceitful kisses of an enemy are set opposite them. A church that has learned to say kindly and truly as one phrase will not have to choose between being loving and being honest, because it will have stopped believing the two can be separated.
roots_summary: Hebrew chesed (H2617), covenant mercy, steadfast love, constantly paired with emeth (H571), truth; Greek philostorgos (G5387), tenderly loving as kin.
roots_lines: Hebrew chesed (H2617) — covenant kindness, loyal love; the great Old Testament word for God's bond-keeping mercy, rendered lovingkindness in the Psalms; Ruth 1:8.
Hebrew emeth (H571) — firmness, truth, faithfulness; joined to chesed in the formula deal kindly and truly; Genesis 24:49.
Greek philostorgos (G5387) — loving with the natural affection of family; Paul's one use of it makes the church a household; Romans 12:10.
usage: “Deal kindly and truly with my master” — the pairing that keeps kindness from becoming sentiment.
“The LORD deal kindly with you” — Naomi's blessing on Orpah and Ruth.
“Be kindly affectioned one to another” — family affection made a church duty.
scriptures: And now if ye will deal kindly and truly with my master, tell me: and if not, tell me; that I may turn to the right hand, or to the left.
Rut 1:8
And Naomi said unto her two daughters in law, Go, return each to her mother's house: the LORD deal kindly with you, as ye have dealt with the dead, and with me.
Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another;

pos: adv. (in a high degree; greatly; with high estimation)
etymology: Old English heah, high, with the adverbial ending. In Greek it renders huper-compounds and, in Luke 16:15, the striking word hupselos, lofty — that which is raised up in men's eyes.
biblical_def: Scripture uses the word to measure estimation, and it warns that men and God do not measure alike. The sharpest statement is the Lord's own: “Ye are they which justify yourselves before men; but God knoweth your hearts: for that which is highly esteemed among men is abomination in the sight of God” (Luk 16:15). The verse does not say that men's judgment is sometimes mistaken; it says that the very thing which stands highest in the market of human opinion is, in that character, detestable to God — because what raises a man in the eyes of men is usually the thing he has raised himself by. Paul applies the same measure inward: “not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly, according as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith” (Rom 12:3), where sobriety, not self-abasement, is the corrective. The word is used positively too, and of one Person: “Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name” (Php 2:9). The exaltation in Philippians follows a self-emptying, which is the pattern the other two verses assume.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines highly as in a great degree; with elevation; with esteem; arrogantly, when applied to a man's thoughts of himself.
webster_full: HIGHLY, adv. In a great degree; as, to be highly esteemed.
2. Proudly; arrogantly; ambitiously; as, to think highly of one's self.
3. With elevation of mind or affection; with great estimation.
corruption_summary: A century of self-esteem teaching inverted Romans 12:3, making a high opinion of oneself the cure for sin rather than one of its ordinary forms.
corruption_paragraphs: The pastoral psychology that entered the churches in the middle of the last century took low self-regard to be the root disorder of the human heart and a raised estimate of the self to be the remedy. Paul's sentence says something else, and it says it with unusual care. He does not command a man to think lowly of himself; he commands him to think soberly — the word for a sound mind, an accurate estimate — and he supplies the standard: according as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith. Self-assessment is to be neither inflated nor theatrically deflated but measured against something outside the self. Both errors are therefore forms of the same fault, since the man who despises himself is as absorbed in himself as the man who admires himself, and both are attending to a question Scripture answers from the outside. The Lord's word in Luke 16 supplies the reason for suspicion. Human esteem is not a neutral instrument that happens to misfire; it is systematically drawn to the things men can produce and display, and those are precisely the things a holy God is not impressed by. Philippians 2 then gives the only road upward that Scripture recognises: the One who was highly exalted got there by making Himself of no reputation.
roots_summary: Greek hupselos (G5308), lofty, high, used of what is exalted in men's eyes; huperupsoo (G5251), to exalt above all; huperphroneo (G5252), to over-think oneself.
roots_lines: Greek hupselos (G5308) — lofty, high; in Luke 16:15 the participle describes what is lifted up among men and is abomination before God; Luke 16:15.
Greek huperphroneo (G5252) — to think over-much of oneself; Paul's coined contrast with sophroneo, to think soberly; Romans 12:3.
Greek huperupsoo (G5251) — to exalt to the highest place; used once, of the Father's exaltation of the Son after His obedience unto death; Philippians 2:9.
usage: “That which is highly esteemed among men is abomination in the sight of God” — the two markets do not agree.
“Not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think” — the cure is sobriety, not self-contempt.
“God also hath highly exalted him” — the one exaltation that followed a self-emptying.
scriptures: And he said unto them, Ye are they which justify yourselves before men; but God knoweth your hearts: for that which is highly esteemed among men is abomination in the sight of God.
Rom 12:3

For I say, through the grace given unto me, to every man that is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly, according as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith.
Php 2:9
Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name:

pos: adv. (completely; exactly; without defect or deficiency)
etymology: Latin perficere, to carry through to the end, from per + facere. The root idea is completion of a work, not moral flawlessness — a distinction that governs nearly every biblical use.
biblical_def: The English word suggests spotlessness; the biblical word usually means completeness or exactness. Aquila and Priscilla take Apollos aside and expound unto him the way of God more perfectly (Act 18:26) — not that his preaching was immoral, but that it was incomplete, and two tentmakers finished it. Paul's appeal to Corinth uses the same sense: “that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment” (1Co 1:10), where the verb is the one used of mending nets and setting a broken bone. A church divided is a fractured thing to be knit, not merely a group to be improved. Thessalonica is told, “For yourselves know perfectly that the day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night” (1Th 5:2) — exact knowledge, of the manner rather than the hour. And the sick who touched the hem of the garment were made perfectly whole, which is completeness of healing. Jeremiah alone uses it of understanding deferred: in the latter days ye shall consider it perfectly, a promise that what is now opaque will be read plainly.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines perfectly as in the highest degree of excellence; completely; exactly; accurately.
webster_full: PERFECTLY, adv. In the highest degree of excellence.
2. Totally; completely; as, work perfectly finished.
3. Exactly; accurately; as, to know a thing perfectly.
corruption_summary: Christian perfectionism reads the biblical language of completeness as a promise of sinlessness attainable in this life, and the Reformed confessions answer it from the same texts.
corruption_paragraphs: The Wesleyan doctrine of entire sanctification, and the holiness and higher-life movements that carried it into the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, taught that a second definite work of grace could bring a believer to a state in which sin no longer remained. The Reformed answer is not that sanctification is unreal or slow-by-necessity, but that Scripture describes it as a lifelong war and describes its combatants honestly. Paul, writing as a mature apostle, says that in him — that is, in his flesh — dwells no good thing, and that the good he would he does not. John says that if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us, and he writes it to believers as a test of honesty rather than of attainment. The 1689 Confession follows this: the remaining corruption abides in every part, whence arises a continual and irreconcilable war. What the perfectionist promises early, the confession promises certainly — but at glorification. The practical damage of the error is twofold: it drives sincere Christians to despair when the promised state does not arrive, and it tempts others to redefine sin downward until the claim can be sustained. The biblical word points elsewhere, to a work carried through to completion by the One who began it.
roots_summary: Greek akribos (G199), accurately, exactly; katartizo (G2675), to mend, knit together, put in full order; holokleros (G3648), whole in every part.
roots_lines: Greek akribos (G199) — accurately, with exactness; the way of God expounded more perfectly to Apollos, and the Thessalonians knowing perfectly the manner of the day of the Lord; Acts 18:26, 1 Thessalonians 5:2.
Greek katartizo (G2675) — to mend nets, set a bone, restore to full order; Paul's word for a divided church perfectly joined together; 1 Corinthians 1:10.
Hebrew tamim (H8549) — complete, whole, without blemish; the Old Testament word for a perfect heart, which describes undivided loyalty rather than sinlessness; Genesis 6:9.
usage: “Expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly” — completeness, not correction of immorality.
“Perfectly joined together in the same mind” — the verb for mending a net or setting a bone.
“Yourselves know perfectly that the day of the Lord so cometh as a thief” — exactness about manner, not hour.
scriptures: And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue: whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly.

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
For yourselves know perfectly that the day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night.

pos: adv. (completely; wholly; entirely — the older and stronger sense)
etymology: From the same root as quit, to set free, discharge, be rid of. To do a thing quite is to have done with it entirely; the modern weakening to rather or somewhat is late and is not the Authorized Version's sense.
biblical_def: Every occurrence in the Authorized Version carries the strong sense of utterly, and the modern reader who imports the weak sense will misread each one. The command about Canaanite idolatry: “Thou shalt not bow down to their gods, nor serve them, nor do after their works: but thou shalt utterly overthrow them, and quite break down their images” (Exo 23:24) — the two adverbs in the verse, utterly and quite, translate the same Hebrew emphasis and reinforce each other. Aaron's rod is laid up as a token against the rebels that God may quite take away their murmurings. Job, at the bottom of his complaint, asks whether wisdom is driven quite from him. Laban's daughters say of their father that he hath quite devoured also our money, and Joab says of Abner that he is quite gone. In every case the word means that nothing is left of the thing in question. This matters most in Exodus, where a partial demolition of the high places is exactly what Israel repeatedly attempted and what the book of Judges records as the cause of the nation's undoing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines quite as completely; wholly; entirely; totally; perfectly.
webster_full: QUITE, adv. Completely; wholly; entirely; totally; perfectly.
The same actions may be quite different when performed from different motives.
2. It is used of that which leaves nothing of its object remaining.
corruption_summary: The word has weakened in ordinary English from completely to rather, and a reader who carries the weak sense back into Exodus 23 will hear a suggestion where God gave a command.
corruption_paragraphs: This is a case where a shift in English usage, and not any theological attack, does the damage. To a modern ear quite good means moderately good, and the adverb softens whatever follows it. In 1611 it did the opposite. Quite break down their images means leave none of them standing, and the verse pairs it with utterly overthrow so that no ambiguity could survive. The history of Israel is the commentary. Judges 1 records tribe after tribe that drove out the inhabitants of the land but not entirely — the Canaanites dwelt among them, and became thorns in their sides, and their gods a snare. Solomon built high places that stood for three centuries because no king was willing to be thorough. The New Testament transfers the principle to the believer's own sin: mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth, a verb that means put to death, not manage. The temptation is always to a partial demolition that leaves the structure standing for a better day, and Scripture's answer is the older meaning of this small word.
roots_summary: Renders the Hebrew infinitive absolute of intensity and verbs such as shabar (H7665), to break in pieces, and akal (H398), to eat up, consume.
roots_lines: Hebrew shabar (H7665) — to break, shatter in pieces; with the infinitive absolute in Exodus 23:24 it is breaking that leaves nothing whole; Exodus 23:24.
Hebrew akal (H398) — to eat, devour, consume; Rachel and Leah say their father hath quite devoured their money; Genesis 31:15.
Hebrew kalah (H3615) — to finish, bring to an end, make a full end; the sense the older English quite was chosen to carry; Numbers 17:10.
usage: “Utterly overthrow them, and quite break down their images” — two adverbs, one demand.
“Thou shalt quite take away their murmurings from me” — Aaron's rod as the token.
“Is wisdom driven quite from me?” — Job, asking whether anything is left.
scriptures: Thou shalt not bow down to their gods, nor serve them, nor do after their works: but thou shalt utterly overthrow them, and quite break down their images.
And the LORD said unto Moses, Bring Aaron's rod again before the testimony, to be kept for a token against the rebels; and thou shalt quite take away their murmurings from me, that they die not.
Job 6:13
Is not my help in me? and is wisdom driven quite from me?

pos: adv. (in part; in some measure or degree; not wholly)
etymology: From part, Latin pars, a share or portion, with the adverbial ending. The word exists to divide a claim, and Scripture uses it where a thing genuinely is divided.
biblical_def: The word appears rarely and each time it is doing exact work. Daniel's image ends in feet of iron mixed with clay: “And as the toes of the feet were part of iron, and part of clay, so the kingdom shall be partly strong, and partly broken” (Dan 2:42) — a divided kingdom described with a divided adverb, and the mixture, not the iron, is what proves it will not hold. Paul uses it of a report he has received about Corinth: “I hear that there be divisions among you; and I partly believe it” (1Co 11:18). The reserve is deliberate and pastoral. He will not pretend to have verified everything, and he will not pretend to disbelieve what he has good reason to credit; he states exactly how far his knowledge goes and proceeds on that. The writer to the Hebrews uses it to divide a congregation's sufferings: partly made a gazingstock by reproaches and afflictions, and partly companions of them that were so used. Some of them were beaten; the rest stood with those who were, and the letter counts both as the same fellowship of affliction.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines partly as in part; in some measure or degree; not wholly.
webster_full: PARTLY, adv. In part; in some measure or degree; not wholly.
2. It is used to divide a statement, assigning one portion to one cause and another portion to another.
3. Opposed to wholly or entirely.
corruption_summary: The honest partly of a man reporting the limit of his knowledge is a different thing from the divided heart, and Scripture commends the first while condemning the second.
corruption_paragraphs: Two uses of division must be kept apart. Paul's I partly believe it is a model of truthful speech: he neither inflates a report into certainty nor dismisses it to avoid trouble, and he tells the Corinthians exactly what weight he is giving it. Christians report far too much either as established fact or as baseless rumour, and the plain adverb is available for the large middle ground where most human knowledge actually lives. The other use is the one Scripture condemns. Daniel's kingdom is partly strong and partly broken, and the mixture is precisely its weakness — iron and clay do not cleave one to another. James applies the same picture to a man: a double minded man is unstable in all his ways. Elijah's challenge on Carmel is the classic form of the rebuke, how long halt ye between two opinions, and the Laodicean letter shows the Lord's judgment on a church that had settled into the middle. The distinction is therefore between a divided report, which is honesty, and a divided allegiance, which is the thing the first commandment forbids.
roots_summary: Greek meros (G3313), a part, share; touto men... touto de, the Greek construction the translators render partly... and partly; Aramaic min in Daniel's vision.
roots_lines: Aramaic min qetsath — from the end, in part; the divided kingdom of iron and clay in Nebuchadnezzar's image; Daniel 2:42.
Greek meros (G3313) — a part, portion, share; Paul's meros ti, in some part, in 1 Corinthians 11:18; 1 Corinthians 11:18.
Greek touto men... touto de — on the one hand... on the other; the construction in Hebrews 10:33 dividing the readers into the beaten and their companions; Hebrews 10:33.
usage: “The kingdom shall be partly strong, and partly broken” — iron and clay will not cleave together.
“I partly believe it” — an apostle stating the exact reach of his knowledge.
“Partly, whilst ye became companions of them that were so used” — standing with the beaten counted as the same affliction.
scriptures: Dan 2:42
And as the toes of the feet were part of iron, and part of clay, so the kingdom shall be partly strong, and partly broken.
For first of all, when ye come together in the church, I hear that there be divisions among you; and I partly believe it.
Partly, whilst ye were made a gazingstock both by reproaches and afflictions; and partly, whilst ye became companions of them that were so used.

pos: adv. (principally; eminently; above all; in the first place)
etymology: From chief, Old French chef, Latin caput, the head. To do a thing chiefly is to put it at the head of the list, and Scripture uses the word where an order of importance is being asserted.
biblical_def: Paul asks in Romans what advantage the Jew has, and answers by ranking: “Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God” (Rom 3:2). Of all the privileges of Israel — the covenants, the fathers, the service of God, the promises, the Messiah according to the flesh — he puts the possession of the Scriptures at the head. The apostle who elsewhere lists eight privileges here names one as chief, and the reader is meant to weigh that. In the closing greetings of Philippians the word marks an unexpected place: “All the saints salute you, chiefly they that are of Caesar's household” (Php 4:22) — the gospel had reached the imperial staff, and the prisoner writing from custody singles them out. Peter uses it to rank a class of offenders: the Lord knows how to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished, “But chiefly them that walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness, and despise government” (2Pe 2:10). All three uses do the same work: they refuse to leave a list flat.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines chiefly as principally; eminently; in the first place; for the most part.
webster_full: CHIEFLY, adv. Principally; eminently; in the first place.
2. For the most part; as, the land is chiefly under tillage.
3. It marks that which stands at the head of an enumeration.
corruption_summary: A refusal to rank — treating every doctrine, duty, and sin as of equal weight — is presented as fairness, but Scripture ranks constantly and calls the failure to do so a straining at gnats.
corruption_paragraphs: The Lord charged the Pharisees with omitting the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith, and the adjective is His: some matters are weightier. He did not say the tithing of mint and anise was indifferent — these ought ye to have done — but He ordered them. Paul does the same when he says he delivered first of all that which he also received, and again when he tells Timothy that bodily exercise profits little but godliness is profitable unto all things. The modern instinct runs the other way, from two directions at once. On one side, a flattening that treats every sin as identical in gravity, which sounds humble but destroys the church's ability to distinguish a fault from a scandal and leaves discipline without a scale. On the other, a flattening of doctrine, in which every question is either a hill to die on or a matter of indifference, with nothing between. Historic Reformed practice keeps three tiers: what is confessed as necessary to salvation, what is confessed as the church's order, and what is left to Christian liberty. Romans 3:2 shows an apostle doing exactly this on the spot — much every way, and then a chiefly.
roots_summary: Greek proton (G4412), first, in the first place; malista (G3122), most of all, especially.
roots_lines: Greek proton (G4412) — first, in the first place; Paul's ranking of Israel's privileges, the oracles of God first; Romans 3:2.
Greek malista (G3122) — most of all, especially; the saints of Caesar's household, and the class of offenders Peter singles out; Philippians 4:22, 2 Peter 2:10.
Greek barus (G926) — weighty; the adjective behind the weightier matters of the law, the Lord's own ranking of duties; Matthew 23:23.
usage: “Chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God” — the head of Israel's privileges.
“Chiefly they that are of Caesar's household” — the gospel inside the palace staff.
“But chiefly them that walk after the flesh” — Peter ranking offenders for judgment.
scriptures: Rom 3:2
Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God.
Php 4:22
All the saints salute you, chiefly they that are of Caesar's household.
But chiefly them that walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness, and despise government. Presumptuous are they, selfwilled, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities.

pos: adv. (with speed or celerity; rapidly; fleetly)
etymology: Old English swift, moving quickly, from a root meaning to sweep or drive. In Scripture the word is attached less to horses and rivers than to two things: God's word and God's recompence.
biblical_def: The Psalmist gives the word its finest use: “He sendeth forth his commandment upon earth: his word runneth very swiftly” (Psa 147:15). The context is snow and frost and the melting wind — the ordinary machinery of a Palestinian winter — and the point is that the same word which governs the weather is the word given to Jacob, His statutes and His judgments unto Israel. There is no delay between the divine command and the creature's obedience, in nature at least. Daniel supplies the second use: in the middle of the great prayer of chapter nine, “whiles I was speaking in prayer, even the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, being caused to fly swiftly, touched me about the time of the evening oblation” (Dan 9:21). The answer was dispatched at the beginning of the prayer and arrived before it was finished. Joel gives the third and darkest: to Tyre and Zidon and the coasts of Palestine, “swiftly and speedily will I return your recompence upon your own head” (Joe 3:4). The same speed that carries the answer carries the reckoning.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines swiftly as with speed or celerity; rapidly; fleetly; with quick motion.
webster_full: SWIFTLY, adv. With speed or celerity; rapidly; fleetly; with quick motion or velocity.
2. Rapidly, as time or the course of events.
3. Used of messengers, of winds, and of the execution of a purpose.
corruption_summary: Because judgment is often slow in a man's experience, its slowness is read as a doubt about its reality; Scripture answers that the delay is longsuffering and the arrival will be swift.
corruption_paragraphs: Daniel 9 is the plainest correction available. The prophet is confessing the sin of his people, and the messenger has already been despatched — at the beginning of thy supplications the commandment came forth. What looked from the ground like a nation left in exile without an answer was, in heaven, an answer already in flight. Chapter ten adds the further detail that a second answer was heard from the first day and was withstood one and twenty days on the way, so that Scripture itself distinguishes between an answer delayed in arriving and an answer delayed in being given. Neither is a silence. The same structure governs judgment. Peter's scoffers argue from the visible continuity of things that no reckoning is coming; the apostle grants the delay and reassigns its meaning, calling it longsuffering toward sinners, and then says the day will come as a thief. Joel's swiftly and speedily is the note that ends the argument: the interval before recompence is not evidence about whether it comes, only about how patient God has been. A doctrine of providence built on the observed pace of events will always mistake mercy for absence.
roots_summary: Hebrew meherah (H4120), speed, haste; yaaph (H3286), to fly wearily or swiftly; Greek tachus, swift, in the corresponding New Testament sense.
roots_lines: Hebrew meherah (H4120) — speed, hastily; the word runneth very swiftly in the psalm of God's word governing nature; Psalm 147:15.
Hebrew yaaph (H3286) — to fly, to be weary with flying; Gabriel caused to fly swiftly at the time of the evening oblation; Daniel 9:21.
Hebrew qal (H7031) — light, swift; used of the swift messenger and of a nation whose horses are swifter than eagles; Habakkuk 1:8.
usage: “His word runneth very swiftly” — the same word that governs the frost governs Israel.
“Being caused to fly swiftly, touched me about the time of the evening oblation” — the answer sent at the prayer's beginning.
“Swiftly and speedily will I return your recompence” — the speed of reckoning.
scriptures: He sendeth forth his commandment upon earth: his word runneth very swiftly.
Dan 9:21
Yea, whiles I was speaking in prayer, even the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, being caused to fly swiftly, touched me about the time of the evening oblation.
Joe 3:4

Yea, and what have ye to do with me, O Tyre, and Zidon, and all the coasts of Palestine? will ye render me a recompence? and if ye recompense me, swiftly and speedily will I return your recompence upon your own head;

pos: adv. (in a manner to excite wonder or astonishment; marvellously)
etymology: Old English wundor, a marvel, with the adverbial ending. The Hebrew pala means to be extraordinary, set apart from the ordinary run of things — the root behind Wonderful as a name of the Messiah in Isaiah 9:6.
biblical_def: The best known use is David's: “I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well” (Psa 139:14). The sentence is the middle term of a psalm about being known — God searching, God besetting behind and before, God seeing the substance yet unperfect — and the wonder is directed at the Maker, not at the thing made. David does not say I am wonderful; he says thou hast made me wonderfully, and the verse before and after both address God directly. The Philistine lords use the word of the plagues: God wrought wonderfully among the Egyptians, and the lesson they draw is that hardening the heart against such works is folly (1Sa 6:6). Daniel uses it of Antichrist's counterfeit: a king of fierce countenance shall destroy wonderfully, and shall prosper (Dan 8:24) — the same adverb of astonishment turned toward destruction, which is the mark of the counterfeit throughout Scripture, that it astonishes.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wonderfully as in a manner to excite wonder or surprise; marvellously; in a manner surpassing what is usual.
webster_full: WONDERFULLY, adv. In a manner to excite wonder or surprise.
2. To a wonderful degree; as, wonderfully made.
3. Strangely; in a manner not to be accounted for by ordinary causes.
corruption_summary: Psalm 139:14 has been reduced to a slogan of self-affirmation, which reverses the psalm: the wonder is directed at the Maker who searches, and the same psalm ends by asking Him to search and try the heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is now printed on nursery walls and repeated as a therapeutic assurance about the self, and taken that way it is nearly the opposite of what David wrote. The psalm opens with a God who has searched him and known him, who understands his thought afar off, who compasses his path and his lying down — a knowledge David calls too wonderful for him and from which he cannot flee. Verse 14 stands inside that setting, and its subject is the workmanship, not the workman's pride in himself: marvellous are thy works. Two things go missing when the verse is lifted out. The first is the argument the psalm is actually making, which is against abortion and against the notion that a life in the womb is anything less than the deliberate work of God, since the following verses describe the substance being curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth and all the members written in God's book before there were any of them. The second is the psalm's ending, which is the part slogans never quote: Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: and see if there be any wicked way in me. The man who is fearfully and wonderfully made does not conclude that he is fine; he concludes by inviting the searcher in.
roots_summary: Hebrew pala (H6381), to be extraordinary, marvellous, beyond the ordinary; the root of the Messiah's name Pele, Wonderful, in Isaiah 9:6.
roots_lines: Hebrew pala (H6381) — to be surpassing, marvellous, set apart from the ordinary; the verb behind fearfully and wonderfully made; Psalm 139:14.
Hebrew pele (H6382) — a wonder, a marvel; the first of the names given the Child in Isaiah, His name shall be called Wonderful; Isaiah 9:6.
Hebrew alal (H5953) — to deal with, work upon; the Philistine lords' account of what God wrought among the Egyptians; 1 Samuel 6:6.
usage: “I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works” — addressed to God, not about the self.
“When he had wrought wonderfully among them, did they not let the people go?” — the Philistines' argument from the plagues.
“He shall destroy wonderfully, and shall prosper” — the counterfeit astonishes too.
scriptures: I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
Wherefore then do ye harden your hearts, as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? when he had wrought wonderfully among them, did they not let the people go, and they departed?
Dan 8:24
And his power shall be mighty, but not by his own power: and he shall destroy wonderfully, and shall prosper, and practise, and shall destroy the mighty and the holy people.

pos: adv. (in security and without anxiety; heedlessly; presumptuously)
etymology: From care, Old English caru, sorrow or concern, with the negative and adverbial endings. The Hebrew betach means confidently, securely — and the Authorized Version chooses carelessly where that security is misplaced.
biblical_def: A word the modern reader will misjudge, because it does not mean sloppy. It means secure — dwelling without fear, and in every biblical instance the security is false. Babylon is addressed in it: “Therefore hear now this, thou that art given to pleasures, that dwellest carelessly, that sayest in thine heart, I am, and none else beside me” (Isa 47:8). Zephaniah uses the same sentence of Nineveh: “This is the rejoicing city that dwelt carelessly, that said in her heart, I am, and there is none beside me” (Zep 2:15). Two great empires, and the prophets give them identical words, because the sin is identical — a self-existence claimed by a city, which is a parody of the name God gives Himself at the bush. Ezekiel adds Magog and them that dwell carelessly in the isles, and says the fire is sent that they shall know that I am the LORD (Eze 39:6). In each case the carelessness is not idleness but presumption: a settled conviction that nothing can reach me, held by a people who are about to be reached.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines carelessly as in a careless manner; negligently; heedlessly; without care or concern.
webster_full: CARELESSLY, adv. In a careless manner; negligently; heedlessly; inattentively.
2. Without care or solicitude; securely.
3. In the Scriptures, of a people dwelling in false security.
corruption_summary: Scripture's carelessly is not negligence but presumption — the settled peace of a people who have concluded that nothing can reach them, which is the exact condition the prophets address before a fall.
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase the prophets put in the mouths of Babylon and Nineveh is worth reading slowly: I am, and none else beside me. It is the divine self-designation, and a city is saying it. This is what unbroken prosperity does to a civilisation — not chiefly that it makes men wicked in the coarse sense, but that it makes them incapable of imagining their own end, which is the specific form of atheism the prophets attack. The mechanism is described in Deuteronomy 8 before either empire existed: when thou hast eaten and art full, and hast built goodly houses and dwelt therein, then thine heart be lifted up, and thou forget the LORD thy God. Amos gives the domestic version, woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and the picture is of beds of ivory and viols and the chief ointments, with the affliction of Joseph unnoticed. The corruption to name is therefore not the enjoyment of peace — Scripture repeatedly promises that Israel shall dwell safely, using the same Hebrew root — but security detached from the God who gives it. The Lord's parable of the rich fool is the same word turned into a story: soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease. That night his soul was required of him.
roots_summary: Hebrew betach (H983), security, confidence — a good thing when its object is God and a fatal thing when its object is the self or the city.
roots_lines: Hebrew betach (H983) — security, safety, confidence; rendered safely when Israel trusts the LORD and carelessly when a heathen city trusts itself; Isaiah 47:8.
Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust, to lean upon; the root, and the great Old Testament verb for faith; Psalm 37:3.
Hebrew shaanan (H7600) — at ease, secure, careless; Amos's woe upon them that are at ease in Zion; Amos 6:1.
usage: “Thou that dwellest carelessly, that sayest in thine heart, I am, and none else beside me” — Babylon.
“This is the rejoicing city that dwelt carelessly” — Nineveh, in the same words.
“Among them that dwell carelessly in the isles” — and they shall know that I am the LORD.
scriptures: Isa 47:8

Therefore hear now this, thou that art given to pleasures, that dwellest carelessly, that sayest in thine heart, I am, and none else beside me; I shall not sit as a widow, neither shall I know the loss of children:
Eze 39:6
And I will send a fire on Magog, and among them that dwell carelessly in the isles: and they shall know that I am the LORD.
Zep 2:15

This is the rejoicing city that dwelt carelessly, that said in her heart, I am, and there is none beside me: how is she become a desolation, a place for beasts to lie down in! every one that passeth by her shall hiss, and wag his hand.

pos: adv. (in private; apart from others; not openly or publicly)
etymology: Latin privatus, withdrawn from public life, from privare, to set apart. The Greek kat' idian is literally according to one's own, apart by themselves.
biblical_def: The word marks the Lord's deliberate practice of teaching His disciples apart from the crowd. On Olivet, “the disciples came unto him privately, saying, Tell us, when shall these things be? and what shall be the sign of thy coming, and of the end of the world?” (Mat 24:3) — the whole Olivet discourse is a private answer to a private question. Mark records the same posture: Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately, and elsewhere the twelve are taken by ship into a desert place privately after the death of John the Baptist. Luke has the returning apostles taken aside privately to report. Paul carries the practice into church business: going up to Jerusalem by revelation, he communicated the gospel he preached “but privately to them which were of reputation, lest by any means I should run, or had run, in vain” (Gal 2:2). He did not spring the Gentile question on a public assembly; he settled it first with the men whose judgment carried weight. There is nothing furtive in any of this. It is the ordinary wisdom that not every conversation belongs in a crowd.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines privately as in a private manner; not openly or publicly; secretly, in a way not exposed to public view.
webster_full: PRIVATELY, adv. In a private manner; not openly or publicly.
2. In a manner affecting an individual, or a small number, rather than the public.
3. Secretly, but not necessarily with concealment of an evil purpose.
corruption_summary: Christ taught privately and Paul conferred privately, but neither made faith itself a private matter; the modern demand that religion be kept private inverts a wise practice into a rule of confinement.
corruption_paragraphs: Two things wear the same word and must not be confused. The first is a method: the Lord took the twelve apart, Paul settled a disputed question with the pillars before it reached the assembly, and Matthew 18 orders that a fault be told between thee and him alone before it is told to the church. That is prudence, and modern church life suffers badly from its neglect — grievances aired to the congregation, or to the wider world, that were never taken to the man himself. The second is a doctrine: that faith is a private affair, proper to the home and the closet, and out of place in public life. This is not the New Testament's posture at any point. What the Lord said in the ear was to be preached upon the housetops. The apostles, forbidden to speak at all in the name of Jesus, answered that they could not but speak the things they had seen and heard, and the book of Acts is largely a record of public proclamation before councils, magistrates, and crowds. The confession that Jesus Christ is Lord is by its nature a public claim about who governs, and a religion that consents to be private has conceded the point at issue. The private conference exists to serve the public confession, never to replace it.
roots_summary: Greek kat' idian (G2398), apart, by one's own self; lathra (G2977), secretly, used of Joseph purposing to put Mary away privily.
roots_lines: Greek kat' idian (G2398) — apart, privately, by themselves; the standing phrase for the Lord withdrawing with the twelve; Matthew 24:3.
Greek lathra (G2977) — secretly, without publicity; Joseph minded to put her away privily, and the magistrates at Philippi wishing to release Paul quietly; Matthew 1:19, Acts 16:37.
Greek parrhesia (G3954) — boldness, plainness of speech, openness; the opposite pole, and the apostolic norm for proclamation; Acts 4:31.
usage: “The disciples came unto him privately” — the Olivet discourse is an answer given apart.
“They departed into a desert place by ship privately” — withdrawal after the death of John.
“But privately to them which were of reputation” — Paul settling the Gentile question before it reached the floor.
scriptures: Mat 24:3
And as he sat upon the mount of Olives, the disciples came unto him privately, saying, Tell us, when shall these things be? and what shall be the sign of thy coming, and of the end of the world?
Gal 2:2

And I went up by revelation, and communicated unto them that gospel which I preach among the Gentiles, but privately to them which were of reputation, lest by any means I should run, or had run, in vain.

pos: adj. and adv. (annual; happening once a year; year by year)
etymology: Old English gearlic, of the year. The Hebrew idiom is miyamim yamimah, from days to days — the recurring appointed season, which is how Israel's calendar was built.
biblical_def: Israel's religion had a yearly rhythm and Scripture records ordinary families keeping it. Elkanah is introduced this way: “And this man went up out of his city yearly to worship and to sacrifice unto the LORD of hosts in Shiloh. And the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, the priests of the LORD, were there” (1Sa 1:3). The second sentence is deliberate: the yearly journey was made to a sanctuary served by corrupt priests, and Elkanah went anyway, which is the setting for Hannah's vow. The same chapter's sequel gives one of the tenderest domestic details in Scripture: “Moreover his mother made him a little coat, and brought it to him from year to year, when she came up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice” (1Sa 2:19). David uses the custom as a pretext with Saul, saying there is a yearly sacrifice for all the family at Bethlehem. Esther records Purim being established to be kept yearly (Est 9:21), and Judges knows of a feast of the LORD in Shiloh yearly. Leviticus uses the word commercially, of a yearly hired servant whose terms limited how a poor Israelite could be treated.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines yearly as happening every year; annual; and as an adverb, once a year; annually.
webster_full: YEARLY, a. Annual; happening every year; as, a yearly feast.
2. Lasting a year; as, a yearly hired servant.
YEARLY, adv. Annually; once a year, or by the year.
corruption_summary: A faith kept yearly — at Christmas and Easter — is not the pattern of either testament; Israel's annual feasts sat on top of a weekly sabbath and a daily sacrifice, never in place of them.
corruption_paragraphs: The Old Testament calendar is worth setting out, because its shape answers the modern practice directly. There was a continual burnt offering morning and evening, every day without exception. There was a sabbath every seventh day. There were new moons monthly. And on top of all that stood the three great yearly feasts at which the males of Israel appeared before the LORD. The annual observances were the crown of a structure, not a substitute for it, and a man who came to Jerusalem at Passover having neglected the sabbath fifty times was not keeping the law in any sense the law recognised. The New Testament keeps the frame and changes the centre: the first day of the week is the day the disciples came together to break bread, Hebrews warns against forsaking the assembling of ourselves together as the manner of some is, and the daily element becomes exhorting one another daily while it is called To day. Against this, a religion visited twice a year is not a smaller version of the biblical pattern but a different thing. The corruption is not in the yearly observance — Purim was established yearly, and Elkanah's pilgrimage is told with warmth — but in the yearly observance standing alone.
roots_summary: Hebrew shanah (H8141), a year; the idiom miyamim yamimah (H3117), from days to days, for what recurs at the appointed season.
roots_lines: Hebrew shanah (H8141) — a year, a revolution of time; the yearly sacrifice and the yearly feasts of Israel's calendar; 1 Samuel 1:3.
Hebrew miyamim yamimah (H3117) — from days to days, year by year; the phrase behind Hannah bringing the little coat from year to year; 1 Samuel 2:19.
Hebrew moed (H4150) — an appointed time, a set feast; the governing word for Israel's calendar in Leviticus 23; Leviticus 23:2.
usage: “This man went up out of his city yearly to worship” — and Hophni and Phinehas were there.
“His mother made him a little coat, and brought it to him from year to year” — Hannah keeping the yearly sacrifice.
“They should keep the fourteenth day of the month Adar... yearly” — the establishing of Purim.

pos: adv. (to each; for each one; severally)
etymology: From a + piece, each portion taken singly. The word exists to distribute a total, and Scripture uses it in the places where an exact reckoning is being kept.
biblical_def: A small accounting word, and its uses show a Bible that counts. The redemption of the surplus firstborn: “Thou shalt even take five shekels apiece by the poll, after the shekel of the sanctuary shalt thou take them: (the shekel is twenty gerahs:)” (Num 3:47). Numbers 7 records the offerings of the princes down to the weight of every spoon, ten shekels apiece. The pillars of the temple porch were of eighteen cubits high apiece. Ezekiel's living creatures had four faces apiece and four wings. In the Gospels the word does two different things. At Cana, “there were set there six waterpots of stone, after the manner of the purifying of the Jews, containing two or three firkins apiece” (Joh 2:6) — John gives the capacity so the reader can compute the volume of wine, which is the point of the sign. And in the sending of the twelve the Lord forbids a surplus: neither have two coats apiece (Luk 9:3). The same exactness that counts every spoon of the princes counts the coats the apostles may not carry.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines apiece as to each; noting the share of each; as, they cost a dollar apiece.
webster_full: APIECE, adv. To each; noting the share of each; as, these cost a dollar apiece.
2. Severally; to each one of a number.
3. It distributes a whole among the several parties concerned.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture keeps exact accounts, and a religion indifferent to numbers, weights, and stewardship is not more spiritual than one that counts.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What deserves recovery is the habit of mind the word belongs to. Numbers 7 is one of the longest chapters in the Bible and it is a receipt: twelve princes, twelve identical offerings, each recorded in full with the weight of every charger and every spoon, and then totalled at the end. Modern readers find the chapter tedious, which is itself the point — God caused to be written down, at length, what each man gave. The same instinct appears when Paul arranges the collection for the poor saints and takes deliberate care that no man should blame him in this abundance, providing for honest things not only in the sight of the Lord but also in the sight of men, and sending a brother chosen by the churches to travel with the money. Ananias and Sapphira died over an accounting lie. A church that keeps loose books, or a Christian who cannot say where his money goes, has departed from a pattern that Scripture sets out in exhausting detail. Five shekels apiece, ten shekels apiece, two or three firkins apiece: the God who numbers the hairs of the head is not indifferent to arithmetic.
roots_summary: Hebrew gulgoleth (H1538), a skull, hence a head or poll in a census; Greek ana (G303) used distributively, so much to each.
roots_lines: Hebrew gulgoleth (H1538) — a skull, a head; the poll by which the five shekels apiece were reckoned in the redemption of the firstborn; Numbers 3:47.
Greek ana (G303) — used distributively, apiece, to each; the waterpots of two or three firkins apiece at Cana; John 2:6.
Greek ana duo — two apiece, by twos; the sending out of the seventy two by two, and the coats the twelve might not carry; Luke 9:3, Luke 10:1.
usage: “Five shekels apiece by the poll, after the shekel of the sanctuary” — the redemption of the firstborn, reckoned exactly.
“Neither have two coats apiece” — the surplus forbidden to the twelve.
“Containing two or three firkins apiece” — John gives the capacity so the sign can be measured.

Luk 9:3

pos: adj. (necessary; requisite; that which is wanted or required)
etymology: Old English nied, necessity, compulsion, with the suffix -ful. The Greek in Luke 10:42 is chreia, need — the same word Paul uses of God supplying all your need according to His riches.
biblical_def: The word's great occurrence is in a kitchen. Martha is cumbered about much serving and complains that her sister has left her to serve alone, and the answer is not a rebuke of hospitality but a correction of measure: “But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luk 10:42). Many things were being done that afternoon and one of them was necessary. Jude uses the word of a change of subject forced upon him: he had intended to write of the common salvation, but “it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). The pleasant letter was set aside for the urgent one. Paul weighs his own life by it, saying that to depart and be with Christ is far better, “Nevertheless to abide in the flesh is more needful for you” (Php 1:24) — a man reckoning his own death against a congregation's need and deciding by theirs. James turns it toward the poor: a word of blessing that withholds the things needful to the body profits nothing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines needful as necessary, as supply to a want; requisite; things needful for the body.
webster_full: NEEDFUL, a. Necessary, as supply to a want; requisite.
All things needful for defense abound.
2. Needy; in want; distressful.
corruption_summary: Therapeutic culture has made my needs the governing category of moral reasoning, so that a duty is weighed by whether it meets them; Scripture uses the word to rank duties, and ranks the hearing of Christ first.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern usage runs the word inward. A man's needs become the fixed point around which relationships, work, and church membership are arranged, and an obligation that fails to serve them is judged unreasonable by that fact alone. Scripture's uses run the other way in every instance. Paul asks what is needful for you and stays alive for it. Jude asks what is needful for the churches and writes the letter he had not planned. James asks what is needful to the body of a brother who is naked and destitute, and makes the answer a test of whether faith is alive. Even the Lord's word to Martha, which is the one text that does concern the hearer's own good, defines that good as sitting at another's feet to hear his word. What the passage does not do is what it is often made to do, namely disparage the serving. The Lord does not tell Martha to stop cooking; He tells her she is careful and troubled about many things when one is needful, and the disorder is in the ranking, not in the work. A Christian who has genuinely put the one thing first will not serve less; he will serve without being cumbered.
roots_summary: Greek chreia (G5532), need, necessity; anagkaios (G316), necessary, indispensable; epanagke, of necessity, in the decree of Acts 15.
roots_lines: Greek chreia (G5532) — need, necessity, want; one thing is needful, and God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory; Luke 10:42, Philippians 4:19.
Greek anagkaios (G316) — necessary, indispensable; Paul's abiding in the flesh more needful for the Philippians than his own departure; Philippians 1:24.
Greek anagke (G318) — constraint, necessity; Jude's compulsion to write of contending for the faith instead of the common salvation; Jude 3.
usage: “One thing is needful” — the disorder is in the ranking, not in the serving.
“To abide in the flesh is more needful for you” — a man deciding by his congregation's need.
“It was needful for me to write unto you... earnestly contend for the faith” — the urgent letter displacing the pleasant one.
