Php 1:24
Nevertheless to abide in the flesh is more needful for you.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.

pos: adj. (that may be borne or endured; supportable)
etymology: Latin tolerare, to bear, endure. In the Gospels it appears only in the comparative, more tolerable, and only on the lips of Christ, and only of the day of judgment.
biblical_def: Every occurrence in Scripture is the Lord's, and every one compares two judgments. Sending out the twelve: “Verily I say unto you, It shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrha in the day of judgment, than for that city” (Mat 10:15). Upbraiding the cities where most of His mighty works were done: “But I say unto you, It shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon at the day of judgment, than for you” (Mat 11:22). And with the seventy: “But I say unto you, that it shall be more tolerable in that day for Sodom, than for that city” (Luk 10:12). The doctrine in the comparative is unmistakable and is not much preached. Judgment is not a single undifferentiated sentence. It is proportioned, and the proportion is set by light received. Sodom, which had no prophet, will find that day more bearable than Chorazin, which had the Lord Himself walking its streets. The servant who knew his lord's will and did it not shall be beaten with many stripes, and he that knew not with few. The privilege of hearing the gospel is therefore also a liability, and Capernaum, exalted unto heaven, is brought down to hell.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tolerable as that may be borne or endured; supportable, either physically or mentally; and, in a lower sense, moderately good.
webster_full: TOLERABLE, a. That may be borne or endured; supportable, either physically or mentally.
2. Moderately good or agreeable; not contemptible; not very excellent or pleasing.
It shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon at the day of judgment, than for you. Matt. xi.
corruption_summary: Degrees of judgment are denied from two sides — by annihilationism and universalism, which flatten the sentence to nothing, and by a popular preaching that flattens it upward so that all guilt is identical.
corruption_paragraphs: The Lord's comparative requires a hell in which sentences differ, and that requirement does real theological work. Annihilationism cannot supply it: if the penalty is cessation of being, there is no more and no less, and the whole force of more tolerable collapses. Universalism cannot supply it either, since a punishment that ends in the restoration of all is not being weighed in these verses at all — the Lord is telling Chorazin its case is worse than Sodom's, which is meaningless if both end in the same salvation. The historic Reformed position holds both truths without strain: the punishment is eternal and conscious, and it is proportioned to light received and sin committed. Turretin and the Puritans taught degrees of punishment openly, and the same Scriptures that teach it teach degrees of reward on the other side, one servant over ten cities and another over five. There is a second flattening, less formal but more common in the pulpit, which insists that all sin is equally sinful because all sin offends an infinite God. The premise is true and the conclusion does not follow. Christ told Pilate that he who delivered Him had the greater sin, and the law itself distinguished the sin of ignorance from the sin of a high hand. To deny degrees is to lose the warning these three verses exist to give: that having heard much is a dangerous privilege.
roots_summary: Greek anektoteros (G414), more endurable, the comparative of anektos, bearable, from anecho, to hold up under.
roots_lines: Greek anektoteros (G414) — more endurable, more bearable; found in the New Testament only in this comparative and only of the day of judgment; Matthew 10:15.
Greek anecho (G430) — to hold up, bear with, endure; the root, used of bearing with one another in love; Ephesians 4:2.
Greek plege (G4127) — a stripe, blow; the many stripes and the few of the servant who knew his lord's will and of the servant who knew it not; Luke 12:47.

“More tolerable for Tyre and Sidon at the day of judgment, than for you” — said to the cities of His own ministry.
“It shall be more tolerable in that day for Sodom” — the sentence proportioned to light received.

pos: n. (a fixed and settled state of the mind; exemption from doubt; that which is established as true)
etymology: Latin certus, settled, resolved, from cernere, to separate or decide. The Greek asphaleia is literally not-slipping — footing that will not give way.
biblical_def: Luke opens his Gospel by naming certainty as the reason he wrote: having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, he set them in order for Theophilus, “That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed” (Luk 1:4). A historian's preface, and its stated purpose is that a catechised man should have unshakeable footing under what he has been taught. Proverbs says the same of the whole book of instruction: “That I might make thee know the certainty of the words of truth; that thou mightest answer the words of truth to them that send unto thee?” (Pro 22:21) — certainty given so that a man can answer, which is where doctrine is meant to end. Joshua uses the word for a warning: “Know for a certainty that the LORD your God will no more drive out any of these nations from before you” (Jos 23:13). And Acts uses it twice of a Roman officer who cannot get at the facts of Paul's case for the tumult, so that Luke, who wrote for certainty, shows a magistrate frustrated in the search for it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines certainty as a fixed or real state; truth; fact; and, in the mind, full assurance, exemption from failure.
webster_full: CERTAINTY, n. A fixed or real state; truth; fact.
Know for a certainty, that the Lord your God will no more drive out these nations. Josh. xxiii.
2. Full assurance of mind; exemption from doubt. Certainty is the perception of the agreement or disagreement of our ideas.
corruption_summary: Postmodern epistemology relocates the fault from a claim's ground to its firmness, so that assurance itself is treated as the sin; Scripture answers by grounding certainty outside the knower, in God who cannot lie.
corruption_paragraphs: The objection deserves a fair statement. Human knowers are finite and fallen; they have been confident and wrong repeatedly; and the history of the church includes real damage done by men certain of things Scripture never taught. That much is true and the Reformed tradition has always said so, which is why it distinguishes the infallible Scripture from the fallible interpreter and holds confessions as subordinate standards, revisable by the Word. But the modern move goes further, and treats confidence as such — not confidence badly grounded — as the intellectual vice. On that account no one may know anything about God with settled assurance, and the only permitted posture is perpetual searching. Scripture will not occupy that posture anywhere. Luke writes so that Theophilus may know. Paul knows whom he has believed. John writes that ye may know that ye have eternal life, using the verb five times in the closing paragraph. The Confession of 1689 devotes a chapter to assurance and calls it an infallible assurance of faith, founded on the blood and righteousness of Christ, the inward evidence of graces, and the testimony of the Spirit. The ground is never the strength of the believer's conviction. It is the veracity of God, and a certainty resting there is not arrogance but the ordinary rest of a creature taking his Maker at His word.
roots_summary: Greek asphaleia (G803), that which will not slip, firm footing; Hebrew emeth (H571), firmness, truth; aman (H539), to be firm, whence amen.
roots_lines: Greek asphaleia (G803) — safety, firmness, that which cannot be made to slip; Luke's stated purpose for writing his Gospel; Luke 1:4.
Hebrew qoshet (H7189) — truth, certainty; the certainty of the words of truth in the thirty sayings of the wise; Proverbs 22:21.
Hebrew aman (H539) — to be firm, to be established, to trust; the root of amen and of the great word for faith; Genesis 15:6.
usage: “That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed” — Luke's stated purpose.
“That I might make thee know the certainty of the words of truth” — given so a man can answer.
“Know for a certainty that the LORD your God will no more drive out any of these nations” — Joshua's warning.
